title: Δαῖς ἐν μεγάροις
titleEn: The Feast in the Hall — Odyssey 20.199–298
about: Philoetius the cowherd greets the stranger, grieves for Odysseus and for the cattle the suitors are eating, and says that he still looks for his master's return. The stranger swears by Zeus, the table of hospitality and Odysseus's hearth that Odysseus will come home while the cowherd is still there to see it, and Philoetius and Eumaeus both pray that it be so. The suitors, who are planning the death of Telemachus, see an eagle with a dove on their left, and Amphinomus proposes that they dine instead. In the hall Telemachus sets the stranger on a poor stool by the threshold, gives him wine in a golden cup, and warns the suitors off. Antinous gives way with a grumble, and the Achaeans sacrifice in the grove of Apollo. Athena does not let the suitors stop their insults, and Ctesippus of Same proposes a guest-gift for the stranger to hand on to a servant.

sentences.t: χαῖρε, πάτερ ὦ ξεῖνε·
sentences.l: “Welcome, father, O stranger;
sentences.i: “Welcome, stranger, my father;
sentences.n: χαῖρε is the imperative of χαίρω 'rejoice', used as the greeting of welcome. πάτερ ὦ ξεῖνε is a courteous address to an older stranger, 'father, O stranger'; πάτερ is the vocative of πατήρ and is not meant literally. The speaker is the cowherd Philoetius, who came in at 20.185; the previous part ends by saying that he greeted the stranger and began to speak. Murray prints no quotation marks, and this speech runs on to line 225.

sentences.t:
γένοιτό τοι ἔς περ ὀπίσσω
ὄλβος·
sentences.l:
may there come to you, even hereafter,
prosperity;
sentences.i: may prosperity come to you at least in the time ahead;
sentences.n: γένοιτο is an optative of wish, 'may it come to be'. τοι is the dative 'to you'. ἔς περ ὀπίσσω is 'at least for the time after': ἔς is εἰς, περ is 'even, at least', and ὀπίσσω is 'hereafter'. ὄλβος 'prosperity, happiness' stands first in line 200, and the contrast with the present, which line 200 then states, is why the wish looks only to the future.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε κακοῖς ἔχεαι πολέεσσι.
sentences.l: but now, at least, you are held by many evils.”
sentences.i: but for the present you are beset by many evils.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is 'but'. μέν, νῦν and γε together press the contrast with ὀπίσσω: whatever the future brings, 'now at any rate'. ἔχεαι is the second person singular passive of ἔχω, 'you are held, beset', with the uncontracted ending -εαι where Attic has -ῃ. The dative κακοῖς πολέεσσι 'by many evils' is a dative of means; πολέεσσι is the epic dative plural of πολύς. The closing quotation mark is kept only because this line is a repeat of an already published unit; the speech does not end here but runs on to line 225.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ, οὔ τις σεῖο θεῶν ὀλοώτερος ἄλλος·
sentences.l: Father Zeus, none of the gods is deadlier than you, none other;
sentences.i: Father Zeus, no other god is deadlier than you;
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ is a vocative, 'father Zeus'. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, and it follows the comparative as a genitive of comparison, 'than you'; θεῶν is partitive, 'of the gods'. ὀλοώτερος is the comparative of ὀλοός 'deadly, destructive', with ω for the ο of the stem, a metrical lengthening that avoids a run of short syllables. The complaint is bold: the cowherd blames the king of the gods.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἐλεαίρεις ἄνδρας, ἐπὴν δὴ γείνεαι αὐτός,
μισγέμεναι κακότητι καὶ ἄλγεσι λευγαλέοισιν.
sentences.l:
You do not pity men, when you yourself beget them,
to keep them from being mingled with misery and pitiful pains.
sentences.i: You have no pity on men, when you yourself beget them, so as to spare them from being mingled with misery and pitiful pains.
sentences.n: μισγέμεναι is an infinitive that says what the pity should have spared them, a use taken from the context, so the sense is 'you do not pity men enough to keep them from being mixed with misery'. μισγέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι, from μίσγω, the poetic form of μίγνυμι 'mix'. ἐπὴν δή is 'whenever, once', and γείνεαι is from γείνομαι 'beget': the ending -εαι is that of the indicative (Attic -ῃ), and after ἐπήν, which takes the subjunctive, it is a short-vowel subjunctive. κακότητι is the dative of κακότης 'misery'. λευγαλέοισιν 'pitiful' is the house rendering.

sentences.t:
ἴδιον, ὡς ἐνόησα, δεδάκρυνται δέ μοι ὄσσε
μνησαμένῳ Ὀδυσῆος, ἐπεὶ καὶ κεῖνον ὀΐω
τοιάδε λαίφε’ ἔχοντα κατ’ ἀνθρώπους ἀλάλησθαι,
εἴ που ἔτι ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l:
I sweated, when I noticed, and wet with tears are my eyes
as I remembered Odysseus, since that man too, I think,
wearing such rags, has wandered among men,
if somewhere he still lives and sees the light of the sun.
sentences.i: I broke into a sweat when I took notice, and my eyes are wet with tears as I remember Odysseus, since I suppose that he too is wandering among men in such rags, if somewhere he is still alive and sees the light of the sun.
sentences.n: ἴδιον is not the adjective ἴδιος but a past tense (first person singular) of ἰδίω 'sweat'; the object of ἐνόησα 'I noticed' is left unsaid, the stranger's wretched look. δεδάκρυνται is a perfect passive, 'are wet with tears', and ὄσσε is the poetic dual 'eyes'. μνησαμένῳ agrees with μοι and takes the genitive Ὀδυσῆος. λαίφε’ is λαίφεα 'rags'. ἀλάλησθαι is the perfect infinitive of ἀλάομαι 'wander', after ὀΐω 'I think'; ζώει is Ionic for ζῇ. The last line is a formula heard before.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἤδη τέθνηκε καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισιν,
ὤ μοι ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ὅς μ’ ἐπὶ βουσὶν
εἷσ’ ἔτι τυτθὸν ἐόντα Κεφαλλήνων ἐνὶ δήμῳ.
sentences.l:
But if he is already dead and in the house of Hades,
oh me then for blameless Odysseus, who set me over cattle
while I was still small, in the land of the Cephallenians.
sentences.i: But if he is already dead and in the house of Hades, then oh me for blameless Odysseus, who set me over cattle while I was still small, in the land of the Cephallenians.
sentences.n: εἰ … τέθνηκε is 'if he is already dead', a perfect; εἰν is ἐν before a vowel. ὤ μοι ἔπειτα is a cry of grief followed by the genitive of the one mourned, Ὀδυσῆος. ἀμύμονος 'blameless' is Odysseus's stock epithet, translated each time; its meaning is in fact not known. εἷσε is the aorist of ἵζω in its transitive sense, 'seated, set'. τυτθὸν ἐόντα is 'being small'. The Cephallenians are here the people of Odysseus's realm, and δῆμος means 'land'.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ αἱ μὲν γίγνονται ἀθέσφατοι, οὐδέ κεν ἄλλως
ἀνδρί γ’ ὑποσταχύοιτο βοῶν γένος εὐρυμετώπων·
sentences.l:
But now they are becoming immense, and not in any other way
for any man could the breed of broad-browed cattle spring up like corn;
sentences.i: But now they are growing immense, and in no other way could the breed of broad-browed cattle shoot up like standing grain for any man;
sentences.n: αἱ is the article as a pronoun, 'they', meaning the cows. ἀθέσφατοι 'immense' is a word whose sense is not certain; it is usually explained as ἀ- plus θέσφατος 'spoken by the gods', hence 'beyond telling'. οὐδέ κεν … ὑποσταχύοιτο is a potential optative, 'could not spring up'; the rare verb is built on στάχυς 'ear of corn', so the herd comes up like a crop. ἄλλως is 'in another way', and ἀνδρί γ’ is a dative, 'for any man at least'. εὐρυμέτωπος 'broad-browed' is εὐρύς 'wide' plus μέτωπον 'forehead'.

sentences.t:
τὰς δ’ ἄλλοι με κέλονται ἀγινέμεναί σφισιν αὐτοῖς
ἔδμεναι·
sentences.l:
But others bid me drive them for themselves
to eat;
sentences.i: but others tell me to drive them for themselves to eat;
sentences.n: τάς is the article as a pronoun, 'them', picking up the cattle. ἄλλοι 'others' are the suitors, who are named at line 225. κέλονται 'bid, order' takes the accusative με and an infinitive. ἀγινέμεναι is a long infinitive of ἀγινέω 'lead, drive', and ἔδμεναι is the long infinitive of ἔδω 'eat'; both end in -μεναι. σφισιν αὐτοῖς is 'for themselves'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι παιδὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροις ἀλέγουσιν,
οὐδ’ ὄπιδα τρομέουσι θεῶν·
sentences.l:
nor do they take any heed of the son in the halls,
nor do they tremble at the retribution of the gods;
sentences.i: and they take no heed at all of the son in the halls, nor do they tremble at the gods' retribution;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι is 'nor at all'; ἀλέγουσιν 'they take heed of' takes the genitive παιδός, 'son' (literally 'child'), who is Telemachus. ὄπις is a rare noun of uncertain sense; 'retribution' is taken from the context, where it is what the gods bring on those who wrong a house. τρομέουσι is the uncontracted form of τρομέω 'tremble at', and its object is ὄπιδα, with θεῶν depending on it. The doubled οὐδέ … οὐδ’ makes two charges: no regard for the son in the halls, none for the gods.

sentences.t:
μεμάασι γὰρ ἤδη
κτήματα δάσσασθαι δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
for they are already eager
to divide the possessions of the lord long gone.
sentences.i: for they are already eager to divide up the possessions of the lord who has been so long away.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the complaint. μεμάασι is the third person plural perfect of μάω 'be eager', with a present sense, and takes the infinitive δάσσασθαι, the aorist middle of δατέομαι 'divide among oneself'. κτήματα 'possessions'. δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος is a genitive: δήν 'for long', οἰχομένοιο the participle of οἴχομαι 'be gone' in the epic ending -οιο, and ἄναξ 'lord'. The man is Odysseus, spoken of to the stranger as someone who may be dead.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ τόδε θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι
πόλλ’ ἐπιδινεῖται·
sentences.l:
But for me this my heart in my dear breast
turns over many times;
sentences.i: But in my own dear breast my heart turns this over and over;
sentences.n: τόδε is the object of ἐπιδινεῖται, and θυμός 'heart' is the subject: the heart whirls the thought around as a man turns a matter over. ἐπιδινέω 'whirl round' is here in the middle, with an active sense. ἐμοί is a dative of interest, 'as for me'. πόλλ’ is πολλά, used as an adverb, 'often, repeatedly'. The dative στήθεσσι is a plural for one chest, and φίλοισι 'dear' amounts to 'own'.

sentences.t:
μάλα μὲν κακὸν υἷος ἐόντος
ἄλλων δῆμον ἱκέσθαι ἰόντ’ αὐτῇσι βόεσσιν,
ἄνδρας ἐς ἀλλοδαπούς·
sentences.i: it is a very bad thing, while a son is living, to go off to the land of others with the very cattle, to men of another country;
sentences.n: The subject of the sentence is the infinitive ἱκέσθαι 'to reach', with κακόν 'bad' as its predicate: 'to go is very bad'. υἷος ἐόντος is a genitive absolute, 'a son being there', meaning that Telemachus is alive. ἰόντ’ is ἰόντα 'going', agreeing with the unspoken 'me'. αὐτῇσι βόεσσιν is 'with the cattle themselves', αὐτός with a dative of accompaniment. ἀλλοδαπός means 'of another country'.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ ῥίγιον, αὖθι μένοντα
βουσὶν ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίῃσι καθήμενον ἄλγεα πάσχειν.
sentences.l:
but this is worse: staying here,
sitting over another's cattle, to suffer pains.
sentences.i: but it is worse still to stay on here, sitting over cattle that belong to others, suffering pains.
sentences.n: τὸ δὲ ῥίγιον is 'but this is worse'. ῥίγιον is a comparative, 'more dreadful', probably tied to ῥῖγος 'cold, shudder'. The accusatives μένοντα and καθήμενον agree with the unspoken subject of πάσχειν, 'for me to stay … and suffer'. αὖθι is 'right here', ἀλλότριος 'belonging to another', and βουσὶν ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίῃσι uses ἐπί with the dative to mean 'in charge of', as at line 209. ἄλγεα πάσχειν is 'to suffer pains'.

sentences.t:
καί κεν δὴ πάλαι ἄλλον ὑπερμενέων βασιλήων
ἐξικόμην φεύγων, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτὰ πέλονται·
sentences.l:
And indeed long ago I would have come to another of the exceeding-strong kings,
fleeing, since these things are no longer bearable;
sentences.i: Indeed, long ago I would have fled and made my way to some other of the kings of surpassing strength, since things can no longer be borne;
sentences.n: καί κεν … ἐξικόμην is a past unreal statement: κεν with an aorist, 'I would have come'. ἄλλον, the object of ἐξικόμην (from ἐξικνέομαι 'reach'), goes with the partitive genitive ὑπερμενέων βασιλήων, 'another of the kings'. ὑπερμενής 'exceeding-strong' (ὑπέρ plus μένος; the English layer has 'of surpassing strength') can carry a tone of arrogance, not praise. βασιλήων is a genitive in -ήων. ἀνεκτά 'bearable' is from ἀνέχομαι, and πέλονται is a poetic 'become, are'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι τὸν δύστηνον ὀΐομαι, εἴ ποθεν ἐλθὼν
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων σκέδασιν κατὰ δώματα θείῃ.
sentences.l:
But still that wretched man I have in mind, if from somewhere coming
he might make a scattering of the men, the suitors, throughout the halls.”
sentences.i: But I still think of that wretched man, in case he should come from somewhere and scatter the suitors through the halls.”
sentences.n: ὀΐομαι 'I think, suppose' has the object τὸν δύστηνον 'that wretched man', and the clause εἴ … θείῃ gives what the speaker has in mind: 'in case he should come'. The construction is loose, as in speech. δύστηνος 'wretched' is pity, not scorn. ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων is 'of the men, the suitors'. σκέδασιν … θείῃ is 'might make a scattering', the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι with a noun of action; it comes to 'scatter'. μνηστήρων here is the first mention of the suitors by name in this part. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A formula of reply: τὸν is the article as a pronoun, 'him', and ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering' goes with προσέφη 'addressed'. πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is built on μῆτις 'cunning intelligence, craft', which is not the same as μηχανή 'device'; it is translated each time. The line is word for word the same as earlier ones. With it Odysseus begins to reply to the cowherd, in his guise as a beggar.

sentences.t:
βουκόλ’, ἐπεὶ οὔτε κακῷ οὔτ’ ἄφρονι φωτὶ ἔοικας,
γιγνώσκω δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὅ τοι πινυτὴ φρένας ἵκει,
τοὔνεκά τοι ἐρέω καὶ ἐπὶ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμοῦμαι·
sentences.l:
“Cowherd, since neither to a bad nor to a foolish man do you look like,
and I myself recognize that discernment reaches your mind,
therefore I will tell you, and on it a great oath I will swear:
sentences.i: “Cowherd, since you look like neither a bad man nor a foolish one, and I myself recognize that discernment has come into your mind, I will tell you, and swear a great oath on it:
sentences.n: βουκόλ’ is the vocative βουκόλε 'cowherd'. ἔοικας takes the dative κακῷ … ἄφρονι φωτί 'you are like a bad or foolish man', which οὔτε … οὔτε turns into 'neither … nor'; φώς is 'man'. ὅ is the neuter relative used as 'that' (= ὅτι), and τοι is 'to you'. πινυτή 'discernment' is the noun belonging to πινυτός 'discerning', and φρένας is 'mind'. τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα 'for that reason'. ἐπὶ … ὀμοῦμαι is tmesis for 'I will swear upon it', the future of ὄμνυμι.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα θεῶν ξενίη τε τράπεζα
ἱστίη τ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ἣν ἀφικάνω,
ἦ σέθεν ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντος ἐλεύσεται οἴκαδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come,
that truly, with you here, Odysseus will come home:
sentences.i: Let Zeus now know, first of the gods, and the table of hospitality, and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come, that Odysseus will truly come home while you are here:
sentences.n: ἴστω is the third person imperative of οἶδα, 'let him know', that is, 'let him be witness'. Zeus, the table and the hearth are the witnesses of the oath. The first two lines are the oath of 14.158–159, word for word. ξενίη τράπεζα is 'the table of hospitality'; ἱστίη is the Ionic form of ἑστία 'hearth'; ἀφικάνω is a rare present of ἀφικνέομαι 'arrive at'. ἦ is 'truly', and σέθεν … ἐόντος is a genitive absolute, 'you being here'.

sentences.t:
σοῖσιν δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἐπόψεαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα,
κτεινομένους μνηστῆρας, οἳ ἐνθάδε κοιρανέουσιν.
sentences.l:
with your own eyes you will look upon, if you wish,
the suitors being killed, who here play the lord.”
sentences.i: you will see with your own eyes, if you wish, the suitors being killed, who lord it here.”
sentences.n: σοῖσιν … ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is 'with your own eyes'. ἐπόψεαι is the future of ἐφοράω 'look upon', with -εαι for -ῃ. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is 'if you wish': αἴ is the epic form of εἰ, κε the usual particle, and ἐθέλῃσθα a subjunctive with the old ending -σθα. κτεινομένους is a present passive participle, 'as they are being killed', in agreement with μνηστῆρας. κοιρανέουσιν 'play the lord' comes from κοίρανος 'ruler': the suitors act the master. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the man, the herdsman of the cattle:
sentences.i: Then the herdsman of the cattle spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is 'then in turn he addressed him', and here the speaker is named by a description. βοῶν ἐπιβουκόλος ἀνήρ is 'the man who was herdsman over the cattle'. ἐπιβουκόλος is ἐπί 'in charge of' plus βουκόλος, and βοῶν repeats the sense of βου-. The speaker is Philoetius again.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ τοῦτο, ξεῖνε, ἔπος τελέσειε Κρονίων·
γνοίης χ’ οἵη ἐμὴ δύναμις καὶ χεῖρες ἕπονται.
sentences.l:
“Would that this, stranger, word the son of Cronus would fulfil;
you would know what sort my power is, and how my hands follow.”
sentences.i: “If only, stranger, the son of Cronus would fulfil this word; you would know what strength is mine, and how my hands go with it.”
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ introduces a wish, 'would that', αἲ being the epic form of εἰ. τελέσειε is an optative of wish, 'may he fulfil'. Κρονίων 'son of Cronus' is the patronymic standing for Zeus, translated each time. γνοίης χ’ is γνοίης κε, a potential optative, 'you would know'. οἵη is 'of what sort'; δύναμις is 'power, strength'. χεῖρες ἕπονται is 'my hands follow', that is, they go with my will. Philoetius answers the oath with a prayer and an offer of his hands.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως Εὔμαιος ἐπεύξατο πᾶσι θεοῖσι
νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε.
sentences.l:
So in the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods
that Odysseus the much-minded return home to his own house.
sentences.i: In the same way Eumaeus prayed to all the gods that Odysseus of the many counsels should return to his own home.
sentences.n: ὣς δ’ αὔτως is 'and in just the same way': Eumaeus does what Philoetius has done. Eumaeus is the swineherd, called συβώτης at line 253. ἐπεύξατο is the aorist of ἐπεύχομαι 'pray', and the infinitive νοστῆσαι 'that he return' says what he prayed for. πολύφρονα 'much-minded' is the epithet, translated each time. ὅνδε is 'his own', with the emphatic -δε, and δόμονδε is 'to the house' with the suffix -δε of direction. The second line is repeated from earlier.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἄρα Τηλεμάχῳ θάνατόν τε μόρον τε
ἤρτυον·
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, while the suitors were preparing death and doom for Telemachus.
sentences.n: ὣς … μὲν and μνηστῆρες δέ set one scene against another: 'so they … but the suitors'. οἱ is the article as a pronoun, 'they'; τοιαῦτα is 'such things'; ἀγόρευον is an imperfect, 'were saying'. Τηλεμάχῳ is a dative of interest, 'for Telemachus'. θάνατόν τε μόρον τε is 'both death and doom', and μόρος is the allotted end. ἤρτυον is the imperfect of ἀρτύω 'prepare, contrive'. The first line is a formula heard before.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσιν ἀριστερὸς ἤλυθεν ὄρνις,
αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης, ἔχε δὲ τρήρωνα πέλειαν.
sentences.l:
but to them came a bird on the left,
a high-flying eagle, and it held a timorous dove.
sentences.i: Then a bird came to them on the left, a high-flying eagle, holding a timorous dove.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but, then'; ὁ is the article as a pronoun, pointing at the bird. ἀριστερός 'on the left' marks the sign as unlucky for those who see it, since a bird on the right was the lucky one. αἰετός is epic for ἀετός 'eagle'; ὑψιπέτης 'high-flying' is ὕψι 'on high' plus πέτομαι 'fly'; τρήρων 'timorous' is built on τρέω 'tremble', so the dove is the shy bird. ἔχε is an imperfect, 'was holding'. ἤλυθεν is an epic aorist of ἔρχομαι. The eagle with its prey stands for the hunter and the hunted.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀμφίνομος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: To them Amphinomus addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: Amphinomus addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: Amphinomus is one of the suitors, since τοῖσιν 'to them' means the company of line 241. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν is a pair of verbs: ἀγορήσατο is from ἀγοράομαι 'speak before a gathering', and μετέειπεν is 'spoke among them' (μετά plus εἶπον). The house reading keeps both, as 'addressed the assembly and spoke among them'. The raised dot introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐχ ἡμῖν συνθεύσεται ἥδε γε βουλή,
Τηλεμάχοιο φόνος·
sentences.l:
“O friends, not for us will this plan run along,
the slaying of Telemachus;
sentences.i: “Friends, this plan will not go well for us, the slaying of Telemachus;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is the friendly address 'friends'. ἡμῖν is a dative of interest, 'for us'. συνθεύσεται is the future of συνθέω, literally 'run together with'; the plan is pictured as a runner that will not keep pace with its authors, and the sense 'will not go well' is taken from the context. ἥδε βουλή 'this plan' is explained by the apposition Τηλεμάχοιο φόνος 'the slaying of Telemachus', the genitive in -οιο. He speaks just after the eagle, though the text does not say he reads it as an omen.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μνησώμεθα δαιτός.
sentences.l: but let us be mindful of the feast.”
sentences.i: let us think instead of the feast.”
sentences.n: μνησώμεθα is an aorist subjunctive in the sense 'let us', from μιμνήσκομαι 'remember, be mindful of', with the genitive δαιτός 'feast, meal'. ἀλλά turns from the plan that is dropped to the meal that is set before them. The speech ends here, and the next line says that the others agreed.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀμφίνομος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Amphinomus, and to them was pleasing the word.
sentences.i: So Amphinomus spoke, and his proposal pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ with a name is a formula that closes a speech: ἔφατ’ is the elided imperfect ἔφατο of φημί. τοῖσιν is 'to them'. ἐπιήνδανε is the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω 'be pleasing to', which has its augment inside the verb. μῦθος means 'word', here 'proposal'. The line is word for word the same as an earlier one.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δ’ ἐς δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
χλαίνας μὲν κατέθεντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε,
οἱ δ’ ἱέρευον ὄϊς μεγάλους καὶ πίονας αἶγας,
ἵρευον δὲ σύας σιάλους καὶ βοῦν ἀγελαίην·
sentences.l:
And having come to the house of Odysseus, divine,
cloaks, on the one hand, they laid down on seats and chairs,
and they were slaughtering great sheep and fat goats,
and were slaughtering fat swine and a cow of the herd;
sentences.i: And when they had come to the house of divine Odysseus, they laid their cloaks down on seats and chairs, while others slaughtered large sheep and fat goats, and slaughtered fat swine and a cow from the herd;
sentences.n: ἐλθόντες is an aorist participle, 'having come'. χλαίνας μὲν κατέθεντο … οἱ δ’ ἱέρευον splits the company into those who lay down their cloaks and those who slaughter. κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε 'on seats and chairs' is a formula heard before. ἱερεύω is the verb of slaughter for sacrifice and meal alike, and the Greek does not separate them. σύας σιάλους is 'fat swine'. βοῦν ἀγελαίην is 'a cow of the herd'; βοῦς may be ox or cow; the feminine ending of ἀγελαίην shows a cow here.

sentences.t:
σπλάγχνα δ’ ἄρ’ ὀπτήσαντες ἐνώμων, ἐν δέ τε οἶνον
κρητῆρσιν κερόωντο·
sentences.l:
and the entrails, having roasted, they distributed, and wine
in mixing-bowls they mixed;
sentences.i: They roasted the entrails and handed them round, and mixed wine in the mixing-bowls;
sentences.n: ὀπτήσαντες is the aorist participle of ὀπτάω 'roast'. ἐνώμων is the imperfect of νωμάω 'deal out, distribute'; the same verb returns at 257 as νωμῶν. σπλάγχνα 'entrails' were roasted and eaten first in a sacrifice meal. ἐν … κερόωντο is tmesis, 'they mixed in'. κερόωντο stands for ἐκεράοντο, without the augment and with the stretched -όω- (diectasis), from κεράννυμι 'mix'. κρητῆρσιν is the dative plural of κρητήρ 'mixing-bowl'. The Greek does not say that the wine was mixed with water, which was the custom.

sentences.t: κύπελλα δὲ νεῖμε συβώτης.
sentences.l: and the cups the swineherd dealt out.
sentences.i: and the swineherd dealt out the cups.
sentences.n: νεῖμε is the unaugmented aorist of νέμω 'deal out, distribute'. κύπελλα 'cups' is a neuter plural. συβώτης 'swineherd' is Eumaeus, who prayed for Odysseus at 238–239 and now serves the cups to the men who are eating Odysseus's stock.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δέ σφ’ ἐπένειμε Φιλοίτιος, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν,
καλοῖς ἐν κανέοισιν, ἐῳνοχόει δὲ Μελανθεύς.
sentences.l:
And food to them dealt out Philoetius, chief of men,
in fine baskets, and Melanthius poured the wine.
sentences.i: Philoetius, chief of men, dealt out food to them in fine baskets, and Melanthius poured the wine.
sentences.n: σῖτον is 'food', grain and what is made of it; σφ’ is σφι 'to them'. ἐπένειμε is the aorist of ἐπινέμω 'deal out to'. Φιλοίτιος is the cowherd of 199–237. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν 'chief of men' is a stock title and does not say the man is a prince. κανέοισιν is the dative plural of κάνεον 'basket'. ἐῳνοχόει is the imperfect of οἰνοχοέω 'pour wine', with an augment ἐῳ- over οι-. Μελανθεύς is the same man as Μελάνθιος.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: The line is a formula for the start of a meal. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα, 'good things, things to enjoy'; ἑτοῖμα is 'ready' and προκείμενα 'lying before them'. χεῖρας ἴαλλον is 'put out their hands', the imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send forth', with ἐπί 'to' standing before its noun. The words are repeated word for word from earlier in the poem.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ Ὀδυσῆα καθίδρυε, κέρδεα νωμῶν,
ἐντὸς ἐϋσταθέος μεγάρου, παρὰ λάϊνον οὐδόν,
δίφρον ἀεικέλιον καταθεὶς ὀλίγην τε τράπεζαν·
sentences.i: Telemachus seated Odysseus, turning over cunning ways, inside the sturdy hall beside the stone threshold, after setting down an unseemly stool and a small table;
sentences.n: καθίδρυε is the imperfect of καθιδρύω 'seat, set down'. κέρδεα νωμῶν is 'turning over cunning ways': κέρδεα are shrewd devices, and νωμάω 'ply, handle' is the verb of 252, so Telemachus is working out a plan; the reader will see its purpose at 262–267. ἐϋσταθέος 'standing well' means solid. λάϊνον is 'of stone'. δίφρον ἀεικέλιον is 'an unseemly stool', not fitting beside the suitors' chairs. καταθείς is the aorist participle of κατατίθημι 'set down'.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἐτίθει σπλάγχνων μοίρας, ἐν δ’ οἶνον ἔχευεν
ἐν δέπαϊ χρυσέῳ, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
and beside him he placed portions of the entrails, and poured in wine
in a golden cup, and to him a speech he said:
sentences.i: He set portions of the entrails beside him, poured wine into a golden cup, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: πὰρ … ἐτίθει and ἐν … ἔχευεν are tmesis: 'placed beside' and 'poured in'. σπλάγχνων μοίρας is 'portions of the entrails', the genitive naming the stuff. δέπαϊ is the dative of δέπας 'cup'. The poor seat of 259 and this golden cup stand side by side. καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν is a formula that introduces a speech: μιν is 'him', and ἔειπεν is the aorist of εἶπον with a doubled ε.

sentences.t: ἐνταυθοῖ νῦν ἧσο μετ’ ἀνδράσιν οἰνοποτάζων·
sentences.l: “Sit here now among the men, drinking wine;
sentences.i: “Sit right here now among the men, drinking your wine;
sentences.n: ἐνταυθοῖ is 'right here', an adverb of place. ἧσο is the imperative of ἧμαι 'sit'. μετ’ ἀνδράσιν is 'among the men'. οἰνοποτάζων 'drinking wine' is built from οἶνος and the root of πίνω, with the verb-ending -άζω, which often marks a continuing action. Telemachus is the speaker, as the verbs of 257–261 show.

sentences.t:
κερτομίας δέ τοι αὐτὸς ἐγὼ καὶ χεῖρας ἀφέξω
πάντων μνηστήρων, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι δήμιός ἐστιν
οἶκος ὅδ’, ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσῆος, ἐμοὶ δ’ ἐκτήσατο κεῖνος.
sentences.l:
And taunts for you I myself, and hands, will keep off,
of all the suitors, since not public is
this house, but Odysseus’s, and for me he acquired it.
sentences.i: I myself will keep the taunts and the blows of all the suitors away from you, since this house is not a public one, but Odysseus’s, and he got it for me.
sentences.n: ἀφέξω is the future of ἀπέχω 'keep off'. Its objects are κερτομίας 'taunts' and χεῖρας 'hands', that is, blows; πάντων μνηστήρων is the genitive 'of all the suitors'. τοι is 'to you' in 263 and the particle 'you see' in 264. δήμιος 'of the people, public' contrasts the community's property with a private house. ἐκτήσατο is the aorist middle of κτάομαι 'acquire', and ἐμοί 'for me' makes Telemachus the heir.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς δέ, μνηστῆρες, ἐπίσχετε θυμὸν ἐνιπῆς
καὶ χειρῶν, ἵνα μή τις ἔρις καὶ νεῖκος ὄρηται.
sentences.l:
But you, suitors, hold back your heart from rebuke
and from hands, so that no strife and quarrel arise.”
sentences.i: But you, suitors, hold your hearts back from rebuke and from blows, so that no strife or quarrel may arise.”
sentences.n: ἐπίσχετε is the aorist imperative of ἐπέχω in the sense 'hold back'. Its object is θυμόν 'heart', the seat of impulse, and the genitives ἐνιπῆς καὶ χειρῶν 'from rebuke and from hands' say from what it is held back; χειρῶν 'hands' means blows, as in 263. ἐνιπή is 'rebuke'. ἵνα μή begins a negative purpose clause with the subjunctive ὄρηται, from ὄρνυμι, 'may arise'. ἔρις is 'strife' and νεῖκος 'quarrel'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες
Τηλέμαχον θαύμαζον, ὃ θαρσαλέως ἀγόρευε.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then, all of them, on their lips having bitten,
marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them, biting their lips, marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.n: ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες is literally 'having grown into the lips with the teeth', the gesture of biting the lip to hold back anger. ὀδάξ is 'with the teeth', and φύντες is the aorist participle of φύω in its intransitive sense. θαύμαζον is an imperfect, 'were marvelling'. ὅ is the neuter pronoun used as 'that'. θαρσαλέως is 'boldly'. The earlier occurrence of this line has ἀγόρευεν, with movable ν; here it is ἀγόρευε.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος μετέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Among them then spoke Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Among them Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke:
sentences.n: A speech introduction that names the speaker and his father. Εὐπείθεος is the genitive of Εὐπείθης, in -εος. μετέφη is the aorist of μεταφημί 'speak among', which is read as 'spoke among them', like μετέειπεν at 244. τοῖσιν is 'to them', the suitors. At one earlier occurrence this line is followed by a word saying that Antinous was troubled; here it stands alone.

sentences.t:
καὶ χαλεπόν περ ἐόντα δεχώμεθα μῦθον, Ἀχαιοί,
Τηλεμάχου·
sentences.l:
“Even a harsh one, though it is, let us accept the speech, Achaeans,
of Telemachus;
sentences.i: “Achaeans, let us accept the speech of Telemachus, harsh though it is;
sentences.n: καί … περ ἐόντα is concessive, 'even though being harsh', and ἐόντα agrees with μῦθον. δεχώμεθα is a subjunctive of exhortation, 'let us accept', with the long vowel of the Homeric subjunctive. Ἀχαιοί 'Achaeans' addresses the suitors as the Greek men of the place. Antinous opens with a show of calm after Telemachus's rebuke.

sentences.t: μάλα δ’ ἧμιν ἀπειλήσας ἀγορεύει.
sentences.l: and greatly to us, having threatened, he speaks.
sentences.i: and he speaks to us with great threats.
sentences.n: ἧμιν is the epic form of ἡμῖν 'to us'. ἀπειλήσας is the aorist participle of ἀπειλέω 'threaten', and with ἀγορεύει 'he speaks' it says how he speaks: 'threatening us'. μάλα is 'greatly'. The threat Antinous means is the warning of 266–267, which Telemachus gave as an order.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ Ζεὺς εἴασε Κρονίων·
sentences.l: for Zeus the son of Cronus did not allow it;
sentences.i: for Zeus, the son of Cronus, did not allow it;
sentences.n: εἴασε is the aorist of ἐάω 'allow', with an augment written εἰ-. The object is left out: Zeus did not allow them to silence Telemachus. Κρονίων 'son of Cronus' is the patronymic after Ζεύς, translated each time. γάρ makes this the reason why Antinous will accept Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέ μιν ἤδη
παύσαμεν ἐν μεγάροισι, λιγύν περ ἐόντ’ ἀγορητήν.
sentences.l:
otherwise we would by now
have stopped him in the halls, clear-voiced speaker though he is.”
sentences.i: otherwise we would already have put a stop to him in the halls, clear-voiced speaker though he is.”
sentences.n: τῷ, the instrumental of the article, is 'so, in that case', and here means 'otherwise'. κε with the aorist παύσαμεν, which lacks the augment, makes a past unreal statement: 'we would have stopped'. ἀγορητής is 'speaker' (cf. ἀγορεύω), and λιγύς 'clear-voiced' tells of a voice that carries, here the speaker's. περ gives the concession, 'though he is'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος·
sentences.l: So spoke Antinous;
sentences.i: So Antinous spoke;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ with a name is the formula that closes a speech, as at 247; ἔφατ’ is the elided ἔφατο. The raised dot ends the unit but not the sentence, which goes on to say how Telemachus took the speech.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ οὐκ ἐμπάζετο μύθων.
sentences.l: but he did not take heed of the words.
sentences.i: but Telemachus took no heed of his words.
sentences.n: ὁ is the article as a pronoun, 'he', here Telemachus. ἄρ’ is the particle ῥα. ἐμπάζομαι 'take heed of' governs the genitive μύθων. Telemachus pays no heed to Antinous.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ θεῶν ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην
ἦγον·
sentences.l:
And heralds through the town the gods’ sacred hecatomb
were leading;
sentences.i: Meanwhile heralds were leading the gods’ sacred hecatomb through the town;
sentences.n: The scene moves from the hall to the town. κήρυκες 'heralds' lead the offering. ἀνὰ ἄστυ is 'up through the town'. ἑκατόμβη 'hecatomb' is in origin a sacrifice of a hundred oxen, and here simply a great sacrifice of many beasts. ἱερός is 'sacred', and θεῶν is the genitive 'of the gods'. ἦγον is an imperfect, 'were leading'.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἀγέροντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἄλσος ὕπο σκιερὸν ἑκατηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος.
sentences.l:
and the long-haired-of-head Achaeans gathered
under the shady grove of far-shooting Apollo.
sentences.i: and the long-haired Achaeans gathered beneath the shady grove of Apollo, who shoots from afar.
sentences.n: τοί is the article as a pronoun, 'they'. ἀγέροντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἀγείρω 'gather'. κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί is a stock phrase: κομάω 'wear the hair long', stretched to -όω- (diectasis), with κάρη 'head' as an accusative of respect. ἄλσος … σκιερόν is 'a shady grove'. ὕπο, accented on the first syllable (anastrophe), stands after its noun. ἑκατηβόλος 'who shoots from afar' is the epithet of Apollo, ἑκάς 'far' plus βάλλω.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ ὤπτησαν κρέ’ ὑπέρτερα καὶ ἐρύσαντο,
μοίρας δασσάμενοι δαίνυντ’ ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα·
sentences.l:
And they, when they had roasted the outer meat and drawn it off,
having divided the portions, feasted a glorious feast.
sentences.i: And when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off the spits, they divided up the portions and feasted a glorious feast.
sentences.n: This is a formula for the sacrificial meal, here said of the Achaeans at the grove. ὤπτησαν is the aorist of ὀπτάω 'roast'; ὑπέρτερα is 'upper, outer', and which cuts are meant is not known. ἐρύσαντο 'drew off' is the aorist middle of ἐρύω. μοίρας δασσάμενοι is 'having divided the portions'. δαίνυντ’ is the imperfect middle δαίνυντο 'feasted', and ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα is 'a glorious feast'. The accusative repeats the verb: 'feasted a feast'.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρ’ Ὀδυσσῆϊ μοῖραν θέσαν οἳ πονέοντο
ἴσην, ὡς αὐτοί περ ἐλάγχανον·
sentences.l:
and beside Odysseus a portion they set, those who were working,
equal, as they themselves received;
sentences.i: Those who did the work set an equal portion beside Odysseus, the same as they themselves received;
sentences.n: πὰρ … θέσαν is tmesis, 'set beside'; θέσαν is the plural aorist of τίθημι without the augment. οἳ πονέοντο is 'those who were at work', the servers, with the uncontracted -έο- of πονέομαι. μοῖραν … ἴσην is 'an equal portion', and ἴσην will be heard again at 294. ὡς … περ is 'just as'. ἐλάγχανον is the imperfect of λαγχάνω 'obtain as one's share'.

sentences.t:
ὣς γὰρ ἀνώγει
Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.l:
for so had bidden
Telemachus, dear son of Odysseus, divine.
sentences.i: for Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, had so bidden.
sentences.n: ὣς γάρ gives the reason why the portion was equal: it was Telemachus's order. ἀνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα 'command', used like an imperfect. The last words name Telemachus: φίλος υἱός 'dear son' of Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο, with the epithet θεῖος 'divine' translated each time. Ὀδυσσῆος has a doubled σ, a form that fits the metre, beside the single σ of Ὀδυσῆα at 239 and 257.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας δ’ οὐ πάμπαν ἀγήνορας εἴα Ἀθήνη
λώβης ἴσχεσθαι θυμαλγέος, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
δύη ἄχος κραδίην Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα.
sentences.l:
But the suitors, the lordly, not at all would Athena allow
to hold back from heart-paining insult, so that still more
grief might sink into the heart of Laertes’ son Odysseus.
sentences.i: Athena would not at all let the lordly suitors hold back from insult that pained the heart, so that still more grief might sink into the heart of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
sentences.n: μνηστῆρας … ἀγήνορας 'the lordly suitors' is the house rendering and sits oddly beside their conduct. οὐ πάμπαν … εἴα is 'did not at all allow'. ἴσχεσθαι (from ἴσχομαι) takes the genitive λώβης, 'refrain from insult'. λώβη θυμαλγής is 'heart-paining insult', built on θυμός 'heart' and ἄλγος 'pain'. The purpose clause has the aorist subjunctive δύη, from δύω 'enter, sink into'. ἄχος is 'grief'. The double accusative κραδίην Λαερτιάδην Ὀδυσῆα names the part first and then the person: grief enters Odysseus, in his heart.

sentences.t:
ἦν δέ τις ἐν μνηστῆρσιν ἀνὴρ ἀθεμίστια εἰδώς,
Κτήσιππος δ’ ὄνομ’ ἔσκε, Σάμῃ δ’ ἐνὶ οἰκία ναῖεν·
sentences.l:
Now there was among the suitors a man who knew lawless things,
and Ctesippus was his name, and in Same he dwelt in his house;
sentences.i: Now there was among the suitors a man who knew lawless ways, Ctesippus by name, who had his home in Same;
sentences.n: ἦν δέ τις introduces a new figure, 'there was a certain man'. ἀθεμίστια εἰδώς is 'knowing lawless things': ἀθέμιστος is built on θέμις 'custom, right', so the man is one who knows deeds that disregard it. Κτήσιππος δ’ ὄνομ’ ἔσκε is 'his name was Ctesippus'; ἔσκε is an iterative form of εἰμί used as a plain 'was'. Σάμῃ is the dative of place, 'in Same', a place name that this part does not locate. οἰκία is a neuter plural 'dwelling', and ναῖεν is the imperfect of ναίω 'dwell'.

sentences.t:
ὃς δή τοι κτεάτεσσι πεποιθὼς θεσπεσίοισι
μνάσκετ’ Ὀδυσσῆος δὴν οἰχομένοιο δάμαρτα.
sentences.l:
who, trusting indeed in his wondrous possessions,
was wooing the wife of Odysseus, long gone.
sentences.i: He, trusting in his wondrous possessions, was courting the wife of Odysseus, who had been gone so long.
sentences.n: ὃς δή τοι is 'he who, you see'; τοι is a particle. πεποιθώς is the perfect participle of πείθομαι 'trust', with the dative κτεάτεσσι θεσπεσίοισι 'in his wondrous possessions'; κτέατα are possessions, and θεσπέσιος 'wondrous' is the house rendering. μνάσκετο is an imperfect of μνάομαι 'woo' with the -σκ- of continued action: 'was wooing'. δάμαρτα is a poetic word for 'wife'. δὴν οἰχομένοιο is 'long gone'.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα τότε μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: he then among the overweening suitors spoke:
sentences.i: He now spoke among the overweening suitors:
sentences.n: ὅς ῥα picks up the description of Ctesippus: 'he, then'. μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω 'speak among', like μετέειπεν at 244. ὑπερφίαλος 'overweening' is the house rendering for the suitors in this phrase; the first part is ὑπέρ 'over', and the second is of unclear origin. The raised dot introduces the last speech of the part.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες, ὄφρα τι εἴπω·
sentences.l: “Hear me, lordly suitors, so that I may say something.
sentences.i: “Hear me, lordly suitors, so that I may say something.
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω, 'hear!', and μευ is the genitive 'me', the genitive of the person heard. μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες 'lordly suitors' is a vocative. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive εἴπω is a purpose clause, 'so that I may say', and τι is 'something'. The speech runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
μοῖραν μὲν δὴ ξεῖνος ἔχει πάλαι, ὡς ἐπέοικεν,
ἴσην·
sentences.l:
A portion indeed the stranger has had for some time, as is fitting,
an equal one;
sentences.i: The stranger has had his portion for some time now, as is fitting, an equal one;
sentences.n: μοῖραν … ἴσην 'an equal portion' echoes the same words at 281–282, where the narrator describes the portion set by Telemachus's order; Ctesippus now speaks as if it were his own idea. ἔχει πάλαι is 'has had for a good while', a present with πάλαι. ὡς ἐπέοικεν is 'as is fitting', from ἐπέοικε 'it is fitting'. μὲν δή adds emphasis.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ καλὸν ἀτέμβειν οὐδὲ δίκαιον
ξείνους Τηλεμάχου, ὅς κεν τάδε δώμαθ’ ἵκηται.
sentences.l:
for it is not fine to cheat, nor just,
Telemachus’ strangers, whoever may come to this house.
sentences.i: for it is neither fine nor just to cheat Telemachus’ strangers, whoever may come to this house.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ καλὸν … οὐδὲ δίκαιον is 'for it is not fine, nor just'. ἀτέμβειν is a rare infinitive; its sense, 'cheat of what is due, wrong', is taken from the context, where the stranger's share is the matter, and is not securely known. ξείνους is plural, and the relative clause turns to the singular ὅς κεν … ἵκηται 'whoever may come', an indefinite relative with κεν and the subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, plural for one house.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε οἱ καὶ ἐγὼ δῶ ξείνιον, ὄφρα καὶ αὐτὸς
ἠὲ λοετροχόῳ δώῃ γέρας ἠέ τῳ ἄλλῳ
δμώων, οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.l:
But come, let me too give him a guest-gift, so that he himself
either to the bath-pourer may give a prize or to some other
of the servants who are throughout the house of divine Odysseus.”
sentences.i: But come, let me too give him a guest-gift, so that he himself may give a prize of honour either to the servant who pours the bath-water or to some other of the servants in the house of divine Odysseus.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come'. οἱ is 'to him'. δῶ is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, 'let me give', and ξείνιον is the 'guest-gift'. ὄφρα … δώῃ is a purpose clause, 'so that he may give'. ἠέ … ἠέ is 'either … or'. λοετροχόῳ is an adjective used as a noun, from λοετρόν 'bath' and χέω 'pour': the servant who pours the bath-water. γέρας is a prize of honour. δμώων is a partitive genitive. The offer reads as mockery, since the stranger is to pass the gift on to a servant. The speech ends here.
